transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

For the last few weeks I’ve just been on this intense high, like I’m wired all the time and can’t turn it off, and it’s starting to scare people at work. It got to the point where my manager and a coworker insisted I come to the emergency department to get checked out.
During this period, have you felt like you were hearing or seeing things that others couldn't, or have you had any thoughts that seemed unusual or impossible for others to believe?

Yes, when I'm working late, I keep hearing this deep male voice behind my left ear telling me I was "chosen" for this, or that everyone would be better off without me if I fail. I've also had this intense belief that I'm the only one who can see the "big picture" and single-handedly save the business. These voices and extreme thoughts only seem to happen when I'm in this revved-up, intense state.
Have you ever experienced a period in your life where you felt significantly depressed, hopeless, or lost interest in activities for two weeks or longer?

Yes, I've been stuck in this heavy, hopeless crash for about three months now, which actually started a little before that manic surge. I've completely lost interest in things like hiking or seeing friends, and I mostly just sit on my couch staring at old work reports feeling like there's no point to anything.
During those three months of feeling hopeless and depressed, did you experience any of those same voices or strong beliefs, or did those only occur during the high-energy periods?

No, those voices and intense beliefs only happened when I was in that high-energy, revved-up state. During the depressed periods, and even earlier in my life, I've never heard anything like that or felt disconnected from reality. It only seems to kick in when my brain is completely amped up.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a clear manic episode characterized by elevated energy, grandiosity, and mood-congruent psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and delusions). The history of a distinct, severe major depressive episode confirms a bipolar pattern, and the restriction of psychotic symptoms to the manic phase supports a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder.
